teachingPoints.text: The lesson introduces the builder pattern through a running example that ends up as a small database-like program holding city residents and where they live.
To model a resident you need a Citizen class plus a separate class for the place of residence, so the domain objects are declared before any building logic.
A citizen's place of residence is allowed to be absent, as for a homeless person, and it is fine for the program to never read that field in such a case.
For simplicity the address is initially represented as a plain string rather than a structured type, keeping the example small.
Residents could also carry extra data such as a name and an age, which are just ordinary fields on the same class.
The example deliberately does not build an object graph: no field stores a list of co-residents, because that relationship can be derived later by a query.
Co-residents can be obtained on demand by walking all residents and grouping them by their house, so storing that list as a field would be redundant.
Residents are required to have a place of residence because the later search method relies on that field to resolve which house each resident belongs to.
The model gains a City type that simply holds the residents and the houses, keeping the aggregate structure minimal.
A full database design would replace the house reference with a house ID that acts as an index into an array, which the author may demonstrate later.
For now the city is built as a fixed structure, and full database-style modeling is deferred to a later part of the course.
Immutability of the city is noted as possible but postponed, since it is a more advanced topic than the builder demonstration.
An init accessor allows a field to be assigned only when the object is created, after which it can no longer be changed.
The city is made immutable so that a created city cannot be modified by accident later in the program.
Immutability means the object's state is fixed after construction, and it brings many benefits.
Immutability prevents another part of the program from silently modifying data that some other component depends on.
Without immutability a function receiving the city as a parameter could not assume that no other code changes the object while it is working with it.
Because the city is an ordinary object reference, another part of the program could otherwise change it during the caller's use of it.
Immutability lets a function or class that receives the city depend on it never changing, both during the call and in the future.
The opposite of immutable is mutable, meaning an object whose state can be modified after creation.
If the city were mutable and a component needed a guarantee of stability, it would have to make a full copy that only it owns, which is far more expensive.
C# offers immutable classes as well: the city can be passed only through the constructor so that it can never be changed afterwards.
A read-only property is visible only inside its own class, so callers cannot change it later, which is why the property is a safer choice than a public setter.
Readonly rules express this same guarantee at the language level, marking data that must not be modified.
A readonly field can only be assigned in the constructor, which makes it impossible to change afterwards and pins the class to the value it was created with.
The city search currently runs fresh on every call, so it does not matter whether the city changed, and this simple version is kept for now.
The search logic could instead keep an internal cache such as a dictionary or even an index mapping citizen name to citizen so lookups avoid rescanning the city.
A cached implementation makes the class silently depend on the city never changing, so the mapping must be initialized in the constructor and every citizen added to it.
The city logic initializes its name-to-citizen mapping in the constructor and simply adds each citizen to it, plus a small guard check.
The mapping approach is built so that another class can later take the city and replace the citizen at index zero with a different one, which mutates the city.
A minimal example city is created containing John and one homeless citizen so the effect of the later mutation is visible.
The city logic searches for John and expects that searching again returns the same John object, which is the assumption the next part will break.
The search call returns John and the code prints that it really is John, expecting every later search for the same name to yield the same object.
The null-forgiving operator tells the compiler the developer is certain the result is not null, silencing the nullable warning without a real runtime check.
After CityChanger mutates the city, running the same search again returns the replacement citizen instead of John, proving the previous result depended on the city staying unchanged.
The logic holds the city object directly and looks up residents by index, so once the city's internal structure changes there is no guarantee the old index still points to John.
Because the logic caches residents instead of re-running the search each time, a city that was changed behind its back yields a different resident than the one originally requested.
This is the essence of a mutable object: we are permitted to go and change it, whereas the same operation would be forbidden if the object were immutable.

C# has no syntax-level immutable array but offers ImmutableArray, which forbids overwriting by index so only reading is possible, and get-only properties would protect the individual fields in the same spirit.
The logic was written assuming an immutable city, but in fact it is mutated, which is exactly the defect causing a resident array slot to be overwritten with another resident.
To make the logic safe, the object it relies on must genuinely be guaranteed not to change from underneath it by some other class.
To be sure the object will not be changed by other code, one option is to create a copy of it with a dedicated copy function, and the other is to assume the object is immutable.
If the immutability assumption holds across the whole program, meaning the object is never modified and is only read or replaced by a new instance, then logic that depends on it becomes simpler.
At this point the city object is in fact still mutable, because individual array cells or objects inside it can be written to or modified.

The object can be declared conceptually immutable, for example with a comment such as "this is an immutable model", and then every consumer of the code takes on the responsibility of not modifying it.
On the conceptual level the object is declared never to be modified, but no C# syntax enforces this, so the guarantee rests only on the convention between code authors.

A get-only modifier only allows the value to be assigned at construction time, while it is still possible to enter the array itself and modify cells, so syntactic immutability is not fully achievable.
Real immutable arrays exist as the C#-specific ImmutableArray feature, but since many other languages lack it, the lesson deliberately does not dig into it.

At the syntactic level the field's mutation can still be prevented by declaring it with a get modifier, or by making it a struct that is then stored inside the array itself rather than in separate memory.
Because the field is conceptually an immutable model, any programmer writing new code must check that they do not accidentally modify it.
For arrays there is no method for adding an element, so even during construction you cannot append a citizen, and you also cannot entirely replace the collection after creation.

Once the object has been created it is fixed, so any desired initialization must happen in that single construction line, even though values such as a prebuilt person could in principle be created earlier and passed in.
After creation everything is locked: nothing can be added even while you are still inside the initialization step, where the object is not yet used anywhere and has not been handed to anyone.
Before going deeper into how immutable objects are installed, the lesson first shows how the initialization is actually performed.

The city is constructed last because it must receive all of its dependencies, so the dependencies are created in reverse order starting from the object with the most dependencies down to the one that depends on nothing.

Right now the objects are independent of each other except that people depend on houses, so the order is houses, then people, then city, and the city must manually list those houses and people into its array.
Builders solve this by creating the city empty first and then filling it with objects, which would look like instantiating a CityBuilder and adding items to it.
With a builder the city would be created through a CityBuilder object into which you add citizens, instead of filling a list yourself.
A citizen is created first and its home is configured afterwards, so the home has to be created before it can be assigned as the citizen's home.
Even though a citizen depends on its home, the home object can be created after the citizen and then assigned to the already built citizen, so object creation order is flexible.
Calling the terminal build method on the builder returns the finished city, so the builder is only a staging area for configuration.
The builder holds a mutable in-progress version of the city that can be filled dynamically, while the produced city object holds an immutable model.
Holding an immutable model is useful because the program can then rely on the built city never changing afterwards.
The next step is to make a chained object-configuration syntax for the city possible, which first requires a CityBuilder class.
A CityBuilder type is the minimum requirement for this city configuration syntax to exist.
The builder's methods should return an object that lets you configure the citizen held inside the CityBuilder, which means introducing a CitizenBuilder type.
The implementation adds separate HomeBuilder and CitizenBuilder types, with the citizen-creating method of the city builder returning a CitizenBuilder.
CitizenBuilder does not yet have the configuration methods, so they must be added, keeping the types as separate, minimally coupled classes.
The citizen builder takes a HomeBuilder rather than an already built mutable home, so the home can be configured further and passed in as a parameter.
HomeBuilder is declared as its own type but intentionally does nothing yet, so at this point only the builder interfaces have been created.
A downside of the current mutable-builder approach compared with the earlier record-based approach is that the program can no longer be semantically sure the required data was supplied.
Because builders are mutable, forgetting to set a citizen's name still compiles, so the mistake is not caught by the compiler.
Such a missing configuration is only detected at the moment the whole city is built, which is tolerable but not ideal.
Ideally the code should report a validation error such as a citizen whose name was never configured, but that validation is left for later.
There are several ways to configure objects through builders, and one of them is the fluent builder.
In a fluent builder the configuration of a citizen is written as a chain such as WithName(...).WithHome(...), with each call returning something to continue the chain.
A fluent builder is one where every configuration method returns the same builder object, so the next configuration can be applied without breaking the chain.
Concretely the WithName method returns the same citizen builder again, which shows that the chaining itself can be implemented in several different ways.
The fluent style can even be built on top of immutable models, which is a common choice when memory consumption of the program does not matter.
Such immutable-model builders are used when memory usage is not a concern, because every configuration step allocates.
With immutable models, calling WithHome creates a whole new immutable citizen model with the home field set and all other fields copied over.
Similarly WithName builds yet another model that copies everything from the previous one and only replaces the name field.
A very common alternative in C# is to accept a configuration delegate and configure the object inside that delegate.
The method then takes a delegate parameter and performs the configuration inside the delegate body.
Inside the delegate the citizen is configured by setting its name and, when present, its home.
The advantage of the delegate approach is that the citizen object does not exist outside the method call, so no half-configured instance escapes.
Because the citizen variable is local to the method call, callers cannot hold or mutate a partially configured citizen.
Переменная John, созданная внутри конфигурационного метода, живёт только в пределах вызова этого метода и его блока.
Второй плюс локального билдера в том, что параметры типизируются автоматически и не приходится заранее описывать их типы в сигнатуре.
Третий плюс: фабрика города может вызвать конфигурационную функцию не сразу, а позже, когда объект уже создан.
Минус: после завершения конфигурационного делегата ссылки на прежнюю переменную John больше нет, поэтому настроить объект после выхода из делегата нельзя.
Дом должен быть создан либо внутри конфигурационного делегата, либо до его вызова.
Если объект создаётся внутри делегата, после выхода из него настроить его дом уже не получится.
Альтернатива: конфигурационный делегат возвращает созданный объект, чтобы вызывающий код мог настроить его дополнительно.
Принята самая простая схема: настраивается изменяемая mutable-модель, которая затем конвертируется в неизменяемую.
Методы конфигурации пока присутствуют в коде, но ничего не делают.
Цель конфигурации: после создания города переданные данные должны сохраниться, чтобы их можно было позднее прочитать, например напечатать имя гражданина.
Пока переданные параметры игнорируются: методы не делают с ними ничего.
Для сохранения данных применяется идея моделей: отдельная изменяемая модель хранит переданные значения, а её результат затем превращается в неизменяемый объект.
Чтобы компоненты не отвечали сразу за всё, выбирается принцип единой ответственности: отдельно данные, отдельно сборка объекта.
Создаётся отдельный класс, который хранит только изменяемые модели города, чтобы хранение данных не смешивалось с кодом сборки.
Такой класс нужно конфигурировать после создания объекта, чтобы затем переконвертировать его в неизменяемую модель.
Для передачи на этапе конфигурации вводится отдельная изменяемая модель гражданина, MutableCitizen.
Эта модель передаётся на этапе конфигурации города, чтобы сведения о гражданине сохранились в собираемой структуре.
У изменяемой модели свойство Age можно задать уже после того, как объект создан.
Именно в этом и состоит смысл изменяемой модели: её свойства заполняются уже после создания объекта.
Для числового поля это создаёт неоднозначность: ноль может означать как явно заданное значение, так и забытое значение по умолчанию.
Поэтому изменяемой модели задают специальное значение, обозначающее, что поле не заполнялось после создания объекта.
Для строкового свойства Name используют признак unset, потому что пустая строка как признак отсутствия значения неудобна.
С Name проще, потому что это ссылочный тип, а не int: значение null однозначно означает, что свойство не задавалось.
Для дома заводится такая же изменяемая модель, чтобы позже можно было задать адрес в вызывающем билдере.
Адрес дома изначально отсутствует и должен быть задан позже, на этапе инициализации города, когда каждому дому выдаётся свой адрес.
Билдер хранит ссылку на изменяемую модель; хранить внутри билдера и сам билдер возможно, но на текущем этапе это несущественно.
Билдер — это объект, отвечающий за конфигурацию изменяемых моделей, из которых собирается неизменяемая конфигурация.
Другое преимущество изменяемых моделей автор обещает объяснить позже, после разбора того, зачем они нужны в текущем решении.
Главная цель изменяемой модели в том, что её можно настраивать не только из билдера, но и из других мест программы.
Открытость полей заставляет посторонний код настраивать их своими методами, что особенно удобно для сторонних сценариев использования.
Поэтому в коде появляется класс MutableCitizen и его модель, передаваемая при создании.
Эта модель доступна как публичное поле, чтобы обращающийся код мог получить её ссылку.
В классе просто выставляется модель и сохраняется её ссылка в поле.
Для дома добавляется свойство адреса, и его сеттер записывает значение в модель дома.
Такой доступ к полям предельно примитивен: можно было бы и просто присваивать поля напрямую, как JohnModel.H = значение.
Выбранные методы — вопрос стиля и читаемости: прямой доступ к полям возможен, но методы лучше отражают намерение.
The Age member could be written either as a property or as a method, and both forms work because it is only a question of syntax choice.
A key advantage of methods over properties is that a method can return a value, for example a future Build method could return the built object.
Otherwise there is no practical difference between a method and a property, since either shape can express the same behaviour.
Methods are more flexible because they can perform validation, such as raising an error when the passed value is negative.
Documenting such preconditions and postconditions in the member signature is called a contract, which states input constraints and output guarantees.
The model deliberately keeps its data non-encapsulated so that code from the other side can reach in and change the values.
Such open access is useful for higher-level programs that do more than configure fields, which is why a good practice is to leave the model non-encapsulated.
Build cannot be implemented yet because the citizen and home models do not exist, so the collection lists must be created first.
The city starts with two initially empty lists, and AddCitizen creates a citizen model, adds it to the citizen list, and returns the built city.
The bare new syntax works without a type name because the compiler infers the type from the method's return value.
Shortening the method to a one-letter name is acceptable here because the method scope is only about three lines, so the meaning is obvious to any reader.
Home.Build mirrors the citizen builder, and the intermediate mutable city object is declared as a public field so the mutable data can be reached from outside.
The mutable city could alternatively be passed in as a parameter, which lets a caller configure it separately and then build.
Build must turn the mutable city into an immutable city model by recursively converting the lists of mutable modules into arrays of immutable ones.
The conversion starts by allocating an array of citizens sized to match the number of mutable citizens held in the mutable city.
After allocating the array the code runs a simple for loop over the mutable citizens.
Inside the loop the code reads the mutable citizen at the current index from the mutable city's citizens list and uses that as the returned value.
The mutable age field may never have been set by the user, so the conversion must guard against an unset value.
Before copying the age the code must check that it was set within an allowed range, and that check is deferred to a later step.
The name field of the immutable citizen is copied directly from the mutable name value.
The Name field of the built immutable object is copied from the mutable model's name, so the immutable value always reflects the final edited input.
Validation of this field is deliberately postponed to a later step of the lesson, and only the naming rule is decided now.
The collection being mapped stores model objects rather than their indices, which is why the lookup needed for Home cannot be done with a simple index.
Because the source collection holds models instead of indices, the builder must keep a dictionary from each mutable model to its converted immutable counterpart.
The author settles on the dictionary approach for resolving already converted homes during the build.
Since the source models are mutable and still being edited, the immutable homes have to be created before serialization starts in the Build method.
The ordering inside Build is fixed: first convert the homes, then serialize the response.
This ordering problem would disappear entirely if the builder referred to homes by identifier instead of by object reference.
The concrete problem is that the mutable model holds a reference to the mutable home model, so that home instance must already exist when the reference is used.
The reference needed at this point is to the mutable home model, not to the immutable one, because the immutable object does not exist yet at this stage of the build.
Every conversion therefore has to start from the mutable home model referenced by the mutable module model.
A MutableToImmutableHome dictionary is introduced that converts mutable homes into their immutable counterparts as the response is built.
The dictionary is created with capacity equal to the number of homes so it is not resized while homes are added.
The dictionary is allocated after the homes are created, and a loop takes each mutable home from the model's homes collection and builds the matching immutable home from it.
At this stage the two home classes look duplicated because each has only one field and differs solely in whether that field is nullable.
The two home classes contain the same single field and differ only in whether it is nullable, which is what makes the duplication look obviously awkward.
The duplication is not pointless design, because the mutable and immutable abstractions can be evolved independently of each other.
The real cost is the large amount of repetitive boilerplate code, since the same conversion shape is written out again for every new abstraction.
After each home is converted it is stored into the response, and the dictionary still has to be initialized.
A second loop over all homes populates the dictionary with the mutable-to-immutable associations.
The dictionary pairs each mutable home with the immutable home that already exists in the response's homes collection, so converted objects are reused rather than rebuilt.
The mutable-to-mutable association exists precisely so that at a later point the already-converted immutable home can be looked up by its mutable twin.
The lookup structure is a mutable-to-mutable home map, and at this point the mutable home is fetched from it when one exists.
A presence check on the mutable home is added and the found home reference is written into the result.
If the builder referenced homes by identifier this lookup step would not be needed at all.
An identifier would work because the mutable and immutable models would carry the same identifier and occupy the same array position.
The converted immutable homes array is placed into the response object for its homes field, and that response is returned.
With the outstanding errors ignored, the build logic now works end to end, so the next step is input validation.
Validation is added requiring that a home always has an address specified.
This check can only be performed at the point where configuration is finished and the immutable object is about to be created, since earlier states are still incomplete.
A null or empty address is treated as an unspecified address by copying the not-specified value before continuing.
When a house has no address the builder can copy the NotSpecified address error into a validation error so the caller gets a meaningful failure instead of asking the model.
The error message can be made precise by naming the index at which the address is missing plus the other field values, which makes debugging far easier.
Alternatively the missing-address case can be detected by searching the residents that reference the house, which catches the object even when the address was never set.
The house-creation method could accept a hidden code-line parameter so the validation error can point at the exact source line that created the house.
After listing many possible richer validations the lesson deliberately picks the simplest option and leaves the others as optional ideas.
The chosen minimal behaviour is to throw an exception as soon as an error is detected, which keeps the builder code short.
A more advanced alternative is to collect every error with its code line and report them all at once for all objects, so one run exposes every invalid object.
The validation pass locates every house without an address and reports each offending object together with the code line where the error was found.
Having a builder abstraction makes it practical to extract a large amount of validation logic out of the mutable models.
In the citizen builder the home is looked up in the mutable home dictionary and taken from it when present, leaving the citizen without a home when the key is missing.
When the caller never sets a name the branch that assigns the citizen name variable is skipped, which means an error must be raised because a name is mandatory for a person.
The else branch of that condition is what assigns the name variable with the field's value, so keeping the assignment only there guarantees names are always set.
In principle a missing name could instead be tolerated and become a builder configuration decision rather than an unconditional error.
A builder setting could supply a default name such as Unknown when none was given, so the validation error disappears in favour of a fallback value.
Because this conversion method is hidden, all of these transformations stay invisible to callers behind a single abstraction.
All of these conversion steps are hidden behind the abstraction, so callers only see the finished immutable result.
A hidden builder method is the right place for any amount of needed validation, checking and transformation logic.
The hidden builder method is where arbitrary checks and transformations can be added as the model set grows.
When no name was supplied the builder assigns the sentinel value NameNotGivenOrCitizen to the mutable citizen model.
Detecting that an age was not supplied works by comparing the value against the sentinel rather than by inspecting an explicit flag.
Instead of checking whether the age is less than zero to detect an invalid value, the check compares the age with the NameNotGivenOrCitizen-style sentinel value.
The check therefore asks whether the field was set at all rather than whether it looks invalid, which is why the sentinel comparison is needed.
After copying the validation code into place the remaining work is to review it and confirm the result is inserted into the response.
The immutable city model contains a list of mutable models for its dependent objects, which is the structure the builder converts into.
The mutable city builder exposes methods that create builders for each dependent object type, which is how validation for those objects is plugged in.
The full city builder keeps the mutable city model as a field, which lets the validation and conversion code read the data it must check.
A conversion method takes the mutable city model stored in the builder class and produces the immutable city model.
That conversion runs the various validations first and only afterwards performs the mapping, so invalid data never reaches the immutable model.
The same validate-then-convert sequence repeats for each nested object, and finally the collections themselves are converted.
The citizen builder follows the same scheme, holding its own mutable model as a field and exposing configuration methods.
The citizen builder deliberately has no Build method, because a citizen outside of a city context has little meaning in this program.
The house builder repeats the same structure, and after that the program can be run to check the result.
Running the program prints John, which confirms the refactoring introduced no bug.
After running the program you can also inspect the created objects live in the debugger, which is a fast way to check the state your builder produced.
The resulting objects can also be inspected in the debugger, where the city object appears as built.
The constructed city contains the citizens and homes that were configured, for example one citizen named John and one home with address 123.
If a citizen is built without a name, building it fails on validation and reports a 'Name not given' message, showing that the builder enforces required fields.
Running the same failing case under the debugger pinpoints the exact line where the error occurred, and lets you inspect other data at that moment.
To demonstrate the next idea the code configures an extra citizen John, age 15, who lives together with the existing John.
Configuration objects that are not needed after the build step can be wrapped in a block scope so they stop polluting the surrounding code.
The home object is only used during the build, so it too can be declared inside a block.
Blocks can also be wrapped into named scopes, which lets a single home configuration be reused for several citizens instead of being repeated.
Currently one home object is created and applied separately to each citizen, so scopes are introduced to apply the same home configuration once.
The scope acts as a separate building block that you create once and then apply inside the scope where citizens are being configured.
When citizens are created relative to a scope, each citizen no longer has to receive the home explicitly, which removes duplicated argument passing.
No matter how many citizens there are, their shared configuration can be written once inside a single scope.
The builder currently lacks a Scope method, so one is added that returns an object exposing Citizen and Home methods with the same interface as the city builder.
The new Scope method returns an object with Citizen and Home members, which still lacks the ability to configure all properties of the citizen inside the scope.
The scope still cannot configure all citizen properties, so the scope's citizen builder needs the full set of configuration methods.
The scope could be narrowed to a citizen-specific one, but a more general scope that works for citizens, homes and anything else is the better design.
A general scope holds the citizen model internally and, besides creating citizens and homes, can set every property of those citizens.
Storing a plain citizen model inside the scope duplicates the builder logic, so instead the scope should store the citizen builder itself and delegate to it.
Holding the citizen builder lets the scope simply call its methods, encapsulating the extra logic the builder performs when populating the model.
An alternative to builder methods would be external static helper functions that configure the model from outside the builder.
Here the configuration logic is consolidated inside the builder rather than in external functions, which avoids scattering the setup across static helpers.
The scope creates an empty model and a new builder, giving each scope its own model and builder pair.
Creating the fresh model and builder can be done at the current level, at the constructor level, or at the factory level, so the choice is left to the surrounding design.
The factory method is only mentioned here and explicitly deferred to a later part of the lesson.
To create a citizen the citizen builder also needs access to the city builder itself, so that scope has to be wired through.
The citizen builder creates the citizen object and then copies over all the properties configured on the model into it.
The citizen created during spawn must copy all settings that were given on the model and then be returned, which is why the method now builds the citizen and hands it back.
The same copy-and-return step is needed for each citizen's home, although the lesson keeps the support narrowed to citizen settings only.
At spawn-creation time the builder passes itself (this) into the citizen so the created object can reach the shared model state.
Putting the builder behind an interface lets higher-level methods work with either the city builder or the simple builder without knowing which concrete object they received.
Both the city builder and the simple builder can create citizen homes because they share one interface that declares the same methods.
The city builder can itself be used as a citizen builder because it exposes the citizen-configuration methods in addition to its own.
Because the city builder keeps the model nested inside it, it shares one part of its interface with the citizen builder and another part with the citizen renderers.
Declaring interfaces for those shared parts lets the remaining code interact through the interfaces without caring which concrete class sits behind them.
With the interfaces in place the code works regardless of which concrete class it was handed, so going through the interfaces is enough for the current state of the program.
Inspecting the two citizens shows that the home field is set on both of them, confirming the copy step propagates the home reference.
Both citizens end up with the home assigned even though only one construction path set it, so the builder path covers every citizen.
If no home is supplied at those construction sites the citizen simply falls back to a default value, so partial configuration stays safe.
One citizen can be given home 32 while another is left untouched, and the untouched citizen keeps the surrounding default.
In the output John shows 18 because his home was explicitly overwritten, while Joe inherits 32 from the enclosing scope default.
Because that citizen was created second in the list of houses it sits at the first index, which the lesson reads off the printed output.
A further citizen created without an explicit home also inherits the home value from the surrounding scope, so defaults propagate to every later creation.
Even a citizen created with no home of its own inherits home 32 from the enclosing scope, and printing it shows that 32 object identifier.
The model currently keeps a reference to the citizen's home object, and that coupling is what the next change removes.
Instead of holding a reference to the home object, a small structure can be created that wraps only the home index.
A struct in C# plays the role of a class here, and the exact runtime mechanism does not matter for this design decision.
The essence of that structure is a thin wrapper carrying just the house index, which removes the dependency on the home object.
A record struct is the C# counterpart of a Java record, which makes it a natural fit for a small wrapper like this identifier.
Declaring it as a record struct automatically generates the comparison and hash methods that would otherwise be written by hand.
The lesson defines a HomeId type that consists of a single field holding the home index.
For familiarity with Java the field is initialized through a constructor that takes an Id of type long rather than an inline initializer.
The HomeId constructor receives the Id as a long value, keeping the initialization in one place like the Java example does.
The Id is assigned through the constructor and stays a plain field with no getters or setters around it.
There is no point encapsulating this single field, so no accessors are written for it.
In Java the equivalent field would have to be private and assigned in the constructor to stop it from being overwritten later.
In C# the field can only be read and cannot be reassigned, so getters and setters here would add nothing.
The citizen now uses HomeId instead of a Home reference, which is the whole point of this refactoring step.
As expected the citizen-creation code stops compiling because it still assigns a home object.
The failure appears specifically in the creation code, which identifies exactly the call sites that must change.
Instead of a reference to the home object, the creation code now passes the home's index inside the city's array of houses.
The citizen now stores the home's index inside the city's houses array instead of a direct reference to the Home object.
Keeping only the HomeId means callers cannot read the home's other fields directly, which makes the current design inconvenient.
A better design makes the home index live in the city and keeps the resolution of index to Home inside the city.
Resolving a HomeId means indexing the houses array and returning null when that index does not exist.
After this lookup the citizen holds an actual Home reference and can be worked with as a Home.
Previously the citizen already had a direct Home reference, so the new design moves the lookup burden onto the city.
Previously the citizen could obtain a Home reference directly, which was a link to the home right away.
The goal is to keep the call syntax as close as possible while not storing a Home reference inside the citizen.
A method of type Home named Get is introduced that takes a HomeId parameter and looks up the houses array by that index.
Putting the lookup in a method encapsulates the fact that the HomeId holds an array index rather than any other kind of value.
In theory the houses storage could instead be a dictionary mapping HomeId to Home, which the method would hide.
Because the storage detail is encapsulated, it could later be switched to a dictionary without changing any code that calls Get.
At the call site the method is invoked as citizen.Get and the HomeId is simply passed in.
The Get method is used as citizen.Get with the HomeId passed in.
If the parameter were a plain int instead of a dedicated ID type, a parallel method for citizens would have to be spelled differently.
A plain int cannot express which entity is wanted, which is why the citizen method had to be named GetCitizen while this one is GetHome.
The HomeId wrapper allows creating an identically shaped but distinct CityId wrapper later, so both lookups can keep the same Get method name.
Methods may be overloaded on the identifier wrapper type so the call site does not need to mention the type.
The citizen's lookup method is named the same way but is overloaded on the ID wrapper type, so no type must be named when getting an object by ID.
Having a CityId means a city can now resolve the citizen object with a plain Get call.
Without the wrapper the city would have to call a separate GetCitizen method and pass a CitizenId.
With a bare int one could mistakenly call GetHome instead of GetCitizen and get no compiler error.
Such a mistaken call silently returns a HomeCity object instead of the expected citizen.
Overloaded methods on the ID wrapper type give type safety, so a citizen ID cannot be passed where a home ID is expected to fetch a home, because Get already selects the correct overload.
The ID wrapper gives two benefits: overloads that remove the need to name the wanted type, and type safety against passing a citizen ID where a home ID is expected.
Preferring IDs over direct object references is at minimum harder to implement than it looks.
Storing direct references is worse because the referenced object graph is harder to construct, forcing dictionaries on both ends of the relationship.
Because an ID is not just an index but a key, you can ask whether the object with that ID still exists even when objects appear and disappear in the dictionary.
A direct reference makes the owner hold the object alive, and switching to weak references only ties the object's lifetime to garbage collection instead of to program logic.
The first of the three advantages of using IDs is that deserialization becomes simpler.
The second advantage is control over lifetimes: when a dictionary's objects come and go, an ID lets you check whether an object with that home ID still exists.
All these entity types, citizens as well as homes, stay flat, so the system contains no references and no object graph and everything goes through IDs.
Using IDs also makes code in the builder simpler because no dictionaries are needed there.
With IDs you can refer to a home by its identifier alone and assert only that a home exists without looking at its properties, instead of handling the whole home class and all its fields.
Working with an identifier narrows the set of actions available to the caller.
The remaining problem is that a citizen's home may or may not exist, so absence must be expressible.
One way to express an absent home is to let a Home ID hold a special value meaning 'there is none', for example a sentinel like -1 that marks it invalid.
A cleaner option expresses it at the type level with a separate OptionalHomeId type that either carries a home ID or carries none.
A second constructor is added that takes no parameters and assigns this OptionalHomeId the special absence value.
That special value, for example -1, is by convention treated as the absence of a home ID.
The sentinel is kept in a constant, such as static readonly NoHome, so that it can be checked later instead of being repeated as a literal.
Writing that static readonly NoHome field is just syntax sugar that invokes the parameterless constructor with the value of the field.
An IsNoHome boolean method can be added that reports whether this home is absent, i.e. whether the default absence value was supplied.
In the citizen type you can now declare the field as an OptionalHomeId instead of a plain home ID.
An additional overload of the fetch method is added that takes an OptionalHomeId rather than a HomeId and returns a home.
Inside that overload the absence is checked: if the ID is NoHome it returns null, otherwise it returns the home by delegating to the other overload that takes a non-NoHome home ID.
This makes the possible absence explicit at the type level rather than something callers must infer.
C# cannot declare at the reference-type level that a value always has a value, so for a non-primitive reference type you must additionally mark it as possibly absent by defaulting it.
The downside of this approach is the amount of extra code required, namely the ID wrapper types and the additional fetch methods.
A further downside is that fetching a home is no longer immediate from a reference you already hold, adding extra steps to every lookup.
Storing a Home reference instead of its id is a drawback because the value must be reached again through the shared context and the quoted database rather than being available right from the link.
Optional HomeId is a nullable value whose getter may return no Home at all, so callers must handle the case where the reference is absent.
The same pattern works at the builder level, where instead of the model a builder carries a citizen id plus a link to the initial builder and passes both along.
Exposing the model as a getter property on the builder, module and citizens lets each of those layers read the model without storing a second copy of it.
Because the id and the initial-builder link are repeated in every builder, it is worth introducing an abstraction such as a structure so each builder holds one field instead of two.
With the shared abstraction each builder passes one parameter instead of two, and the duplication logic is encapsulated in a separate type reused by all later builder types for different objects.
The concrete gain is that the Build method no longer has to build those dictionaries of relations for each type, because the identifiers are already at hand.
If each type has its identifier available directly instead of a link to Home, the relation dictionaries become unnecessary and the slot stores just the id.
The remaining code keeps working unchanged because the model is now read through the home reference itself rather than from a stored model instance.
The lesson then moves on to removing duplicated code with interfaces, noting that the same methods had to be repeated in the copy builder and in the citizen builder.
The same methods are repeated verbatim in the copy builder and in the citizen builder, which is the duplication the lesson wants to eliminate.

C# has no default interface implementation to share the code, so the deduplication is done with extension methods: methods declared outside the class they apply to while keeping the ordinary call syntax.
A citizen builder interface is introduced that declares only a Model getter, and the builder stores the model it is meant to configure behind that getter.
The shared configuration methods are moved into a separate static class named CitizenBuilderExtensions so they are declared once instead of per builder.
From now on the base methods live on these separate static configuration methods rather than being written on the builder class itself.
The extension methods receive the builder through the new interface, which requires adding this before the type of the first parameter so they are recognized as extension methods.
The interface member is implemented as a getter, and the syntax Model with get creates both a field of the model and a get method that returns that field, which the builder then assigns.
Instead of the explicit field plus method you can declare a read-only property with only a get and assign it in the constructor, and the compiler itself generates the hidden backing field.
The builder must expose the same read-only model getter so the shared extension methods can read the model it is configuring.
The builder is the only place that hands the configured model back to the caller, so returning it from there is what makes the fluent chain work.
The surrounding code stays exactly as it was because no new implementation was added: the class already has to implement IEnumerable for its own reasons.
Introducing virtual method calls for the fields does not by itself remove all duplication, but it lets the field-setting logic be reorganized.
Moving the field-assignment methods out of the model into the builder means those fields are no longer duplicated in the class that lets you configure a group of objects.
A name like CitizenBuilder is a convention meaning the configuration method returns the same builder instance so calls can be chained fluently.
A builder configuration method returns the very same builder object rather than a new copy, which is what allows chaining calls on one expression.
Because the builder returns itself, you can configure an age and a name of a freshly created citizen inline within a single statement.
Builders bring little real benefit here and usually complicate debugging, because several operations collapse into one line and no breakpoint can be placed in the middle of the chained expression.
When a chained call throws, the stack trace only points at the combined line, so you cannot tell which method inside the chain actually failed.
The main gain of the fluent builder is more compact code: no intermediate variable is needed and the object no longer has to be built up separately.
Builders are also used for wrapping many objects, where the builder can be treated at any moment as if it were the final ready object.
Builders appear when an object is wrapped in another wrapper several layers deep, so that at every nesting level the object being built can still be used as it currently is.
An abstract builder may mean a builder that works with its own model type instead of the shared model, which lets independent builders coexist.
An abstract builder may also mean a builder that produces its own type of object rather than the shared one.
When builders hold different models you interact with them through an interface, and the builder exposes only configuration methods with no direct access to the model.
A citizen builder can be consumed through an interface that declares the three configuration methods and returns the interface rather than a concrete builder instance.
To make a city builder follow that interface you declare the builder class as implementing it and implement the interface methods inside the builder.
Explicit interface implementation lets you keep an overload that returns the concrete builder type while the interface-typed call returns the less specific type.
This is done so the information that you are working with a specific builder type is preserved when you call it directly, rather than only through the interface.
A builder keeps track of which concrete builder type created it, which matters when the concrete CityBuilder type is used directly instead of through the interface.
Implementing the interface for CityBuilder is awkward because WithHome accepts a HomeBuilder parameter, so the method must verify that the builder it was handed is the expected concrete type.

Depending on the exact builder type weakens the type system, because a caller could pass a different HomeBuilder even though the code assumes it came from the same builder that produced this CityBuilder.
The same method can instead be written as an explicit interface implementation so CityBuilder takes the parameter, checks whether it is the required type and calls Home with the correct type.
Working with the concrete CityBuilder directly keeps exactly the same behavior as before, because the interface implementation changed nothing here.
Because both builders expose the same interface, client code can use CityBuilder through that interface instead of the concrete type.
CityBuilder is also missing the Scope member, so an ICityBuilder interface is introduced for it just like for the other builder.
The members shared by the two builders, and therefore the ones duplicated when each gets its own interface, are WithHome and WithCity.
The shared WithHome and WithCity logic could be generalized into a common interface so the same methods are not duplicated in two places.
After that generalization the implementations keep all of their members, call the other builder's Scope, and only WithHome actually differs.
The interfaces could additionally be made to inherit from the concrete builder types, which in principle would remove most of the casts.

Because the model is now stored through interfaces, the way and place each implementation keeps its data can be changed freely: one model, separate fields, another location, or entirely different models.
Interfaces should not be introduced when that flexibility about where the data lives is not actually required.
The cost of an interface is the extra code it adds, and all of that code has to be maintained afterwards.
It is better not to plan ahead for a possible future need to swap in a different model, because that code would have to be maintained even if the need never arises.
When new functionality is needed it may well be easier to make the existing class more general than to make everything abstract and hide it behind interfaces.
Build can return different model types depending on which abstract builder you use, so its return type has to accommodate those variants.
Declaring C as an abstract class rather than an interface would let each concrete CityBuilder implementation create its own city.

Each concrete builder implementation creates its own City implementation, and that shared contract is best expressed as an interface (ICity) exposing operations such as getting a city or a home by ID.
Every City implementation must implement the shared interface, so a default one can keep data in arrays while a dynamic one keeps it in dictionaries or sparse sets.
Both implementations store cities and homes under the same keys and satisfy the same interface, differing only in how they pull values out of their underlying collections.
Different builder classes can override Build so that each produces a different City implementation, which here means the default one.
Because builder classes can each override Build, the main Build here returns a default City implementation.
Inside the interface there will be an ICity contract, and the concrete class C implements I by supplying the methods with array-backed behavior.
A sibling builder subclass can implement the same method with its own model and build its City implementation differently.
The pattern can be split into a builder part and a final-object-creation part, giving two separate objects whose creation methods properly initialize the builder.
A CityFinalBuilder exposes only Build and references the same CityBuilder, which handles configuration, so the final object can be produced from the configured builder.
At the end you invoke Build through the final builder so the produced City implementation is built from the configured builder rather than a fresh default one.
